extracted.intended_audience: children's and young-adult authors/illustrators, librarians, award researchers, and general readers interested in literary awards
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of the standards and descriptive criteria used by / associated with the Coretta Scott King Book Award: what the award recognizes, who is eligible, award categories (author, illustrator, honors), related lifetime/new-talent awards, and presentation/recognition conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: The most distinguished portrayal of African American experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Awarded for: The most distinguished portrayal of African American experience in literature for children or teens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The award "recognizes outstanding books for young adults and children by African Americans that reflect the African American experience." This is the primary substantive standard against which works are identified as winners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Works must be by African Americans (creator eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: The award recognizes outstanding books for young adults and children by African Americans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page frames the award as presented to authors and illustrators 'by African Americans'—i.e., creator identity (African American) is integral to eligibility/intent of the prize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awards given to authors and illustrators; Honor Books as runner-ups
rubrics_metrics.description: Awards are given both to authors and to illustrators; starting in 1978 runner-up Author Honor Books have been recognized and recognition of runner-up Illustrator Honor Books began in 1981.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes categories (author vs. illustrator) and type of recognition (Winner vs. Honor). Historically, the program added illustrator category in 1974 and Honor Book recognition in different years for author and illustrator categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of universal human values
rubrics_metrics.description: Awards are given both to authors and to illustrators for universal human values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond portraying African American experience, the page signals that recognized works exemplify universal human values—this is cited as part of the rationale for selection and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal selection criteria aligned with ALA standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Effie Lee Morris wrote formal selection criteria for the awards to meet ALA's standards, and the Coretta Scott King Awards were accepted as an ALA unit award in 1982.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the page does not reproduce the full ALA-aligned criteria, it documents that formalized selection standards exist and that the award's procedures were developed to comply with American Library Association expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: John Steptoe Award for New Talent (new-talent eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning in 1996 an occasional John Steptoe Award for New Talent has been given; from 1996 on the program includes the John Steptoe Award for New Talent, optionally awarded to an author, an illustrator, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a related criterion/program for identifying emerging creators: the award recognizes "new talent" and can be conferred on authors, illustrators, or both. The page does not specify detailed eligibility rules beyond its focus on new talent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coretta Scott King–Virginia Hamilton Award for Lifetime Achievement (presentation criteria)
rubrics_metrics.description: From 2010 the program includes the Coretta Scott King–Virginia Hamilton Award for Lifetime Achievement. It is presented to creators and practitioners alternately: in even years, to an African American writer or illustrator of books for children or young adults; in odd years, to a practitioner for 'active engagement with youth using award-winning African American literature for children and/or young adults, via implementation of reading and reading related activities/programs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes explicit alternation and the two distinct types of recipients (creators vs. practitioners engaged with youth), and therefore defines selection axes for the lifetime-achievement recognition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation and recognition standards (medal, certificate, seal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Winning books receive a medal; honor books receive a certificate. Winning and honor books are identified by the presence on their covers of the Coretta Scott King Award Seal. The original seal was designed in 1974 (bronze seal on winning books and a pewter seal on honor books); later revisions changed colors to bronze and black for winners, and pewter and black for honors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the physical forms of recognition and the seal conventions applied to winning and honor titles; useful for producers/publishers and for identifying awarded editions.
